stories.headline: India counters China in Nepal amid flood crisis
stories.title: India counters China in Nepal amid flood crisis
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Relations had frayed over the past decade amid border disputes and resentment over a 2015 blockade that many Nepalis blamed on New Delhi and which crippled fuel and other supplies.
India has denied it was responsible.

Over the same period, China expanded its footprint, with trade surging as electronics and electric vehicles flooded Nepali markets and Beijing extended its influence through infrastructure, health and education.
Land-locked Nepal is nestled in the Himalayas between China and India and the two Asian giants have vied for influence in the impoverished nation for decades.

China's economic rise has given Kathmandu greater room to manoeuvre between its neighbours, challenging India's longstanding assumption that geography, economic integration and cultural ties between the two Hindu-majority countries would preserve its primacy.
The floods have given Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi an opening to claw back some lost ground in the battle for influence.
India was the first foreign government to respond to one of Nepal's worst recorded disasters in August, sending relief supplies and helping restore communications.
On Monday, New Delhi followed with a $1.62 billion package of grants and credit for reconstruction, infrastructure and energy.
India extended the package when 36-year-old Shah came to New Delhi, his first bilateral visit since taking power in March.
Nepal needs about $5 billion to rebuild damaged infrastructure, nearly a tenth of its economy.
India's package is the largest financial assistance Nepal has ever received, Minister for Foreign Affairs Shisir Khanal said in a statement.
Indian aid disbursement to Nepal was over fourfold higher than that of China in the 2024-25 fiscal year that ended in mid-July, according to Nepali government data.

stories.headline: ISI widens spy network across India, puts Bengal military bases in focus
stories.title: ISI widens spy network across India, puts Bengal military bases in focus
stories.summary: Following Operation Sindoor, launched by the Indian armed forces in retaliation for the Pahalgam terror attack, attempts have been made to intensify terrorist activities in India.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'terror attack' in summary weight 50.4
article_sentences: Following Operation Sindoor, launched by the Indian armed forces in retaliation for the Pahalgam terror attack, attempts have been made to intensify terrorist activities in India.
New Delhi: Pakistan has been employing every possible tactic to gain an advantage over India.

Its desperation has intensified since Operation Sindoor, during which the Indian armed forces dealt severe blows to its key terror proxies, the Lashkar-e-Taiba, Jaish-e-Mohammed and Hizbul Mujahideen.
The Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) has reportedly taken direct control of the three terror outfits and brought them under a unified command structure to coordinate their operations.
Intelligence agencies have flagged concerns about the rising espionage activity that the ISI is involved in against India.
An Intelligence Bureau official said that the ISI’s espionage racket focused more on Jammu and Kashmir, Punjab, Rajasthan and Delhi.

“Although attempts to carry out espionage activities continue in different parts of the country, fresh intelligence inputs indicate that military installations in West Bengal are now a major focus,” the official said.
Between August and November this year, five arrests have been made, and preliminary investigations reveal that they are the ISI’s assets.
In August, three persons were arrested in Dinhata over suspected ISI links.
The probe against them is focused on the alleged procurement of SIM cards and attempts to circulate fake currency.
The arrests in November this year point directly to espionage activity where the brief was to gather sensitive information relating to the Indian military.
Ashraful Alam, who was arrested near Bagdogra airport in Siliguri, West Bengal, allegedly posed as a beggar to gather sensitive information.

stories.headline: The Pursuit of longevity: India embraces wellness retreats to live better
stories.title: The Pursuit of longevity: India embraces wellness retreats to live better
stories.summary: Before Rohan and Rishabh Jain built a wellness company, they were professional tennis players. After studying abroad, the brothers returned to India and found only a few facilities offering specialised recovery and rejuvenation therapies such as cold therapy, red-light therapy, and IV-based therapy. In 2021, they started The Wellness Co, a multi-city, membership-based clinic model for science-backed recovery and longevity solutions.After expanding their wellness clinics to eight cities, the bootstrapped business moved into retreats in July, opening a 270-acre facility at Karma Lakelands in Gurugram, which it claims is the first luxury longevity retreat in India. “We decided to expand into the retreat space to create a programme where people could focus on wellness 24 hours a day and to offer an integrative experience with daily consultations, diet and nutrition, ayurveda—putting in a system and protocol personalised to the individuals,” says Rishabh. The company is now planning a facility in Landour, Mussoorie, and is in discussions for similar retreats in Bengaluru and Goa.For a luxury, longevity-focused vacation, guests are paying to know themselves—and their bodies—in detail. These retreats bring together luxury hospitality and cutting-edge wellness science, offering guests access to personalised biohacking protocols, advanced diagnostics and therapies designed to optimise their health and potentially extend their healthspan. In this emerging picture of luxury, the ultimate indulgence is no longer simply escaping to an island or a secluded property, but returning healthier, better rested, and with a deeper understanding of one’s body.Also Read: The new longevity hack: Not to live forever, but better for longerBy the time one arrives, the programme has been written for them. Dr Garima Gaur, chief wellness officer at The Wellness Co, describes how it starts. “When a person signs up for a retreat, the first consultation with the doctor is done online to understand what concerns the patient has, what their current lifestyle is like, what is that they would like to work on, and what their barriers are. We sometimes recommend a basic blood test or profiling for nutrients. Based on this, an entire programme is customised for them and we let our team know of the customised protocol along with the nutrition requirements for the duration of the stay.”A spa day, an ayurveda massage or a yoga break no longer satisfy a growing set of Indians who want to biohack their way to a healthier old age. They want wellness they can measure: Biomarkers brought back to healthy levels, and the biological age of their organs wound back.Also Read: What Are Peptide Parties? The Wellness Trend Behind Bengaluru's CrackdownThe trend is also evolving against India’s growing medical and wellness tourism economy. According to reports, India’s medical tourism market was estimated at $8.7 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $16.2 billion by 2030. The larger global Medical Value Travel market, valued at approximately $115.6 billion in 2022, is expected to reach $286.1 billion by 2030. India already ranks 12th among the world’s top 20 wellness tourism markets and fifth among the top 10 wellness destinations in the Asia-Pacific region, according to the Medical Tourism Index 2020-21. The Wellness Co Karma Lakelands offers science-backed wellness therapies for those striving for peak health, performance, and longevityWhile medical tourism has traditionally been associated with curative treatments and specialised procedures, wellness tourism is increasingly centred on prevention, recovery, and holistic well-being. For India’s emerging luxury wellness segment, traditional practices such as ayurveda, yoga and naturopathy are now finding space alongside modern diagnostics, personalised nutrition and recovery therapies. The government, through initiatives such as ‘Heal in India’ and the dedicated AYUSH Visa introduced in July 2023, is also looking to strengthen India’s position as a destination for integrated healthcare and preventive wellness.For luxury hospitality players, this presents an opportunity to move beyond conventional spa-led offerings and create longer, purpose-driven stays where the real indulgence is investing in one’s health and longevity.Also Read: Is India's healthcare industry ready for the 'longevity' disruption? Deepak Saini weighs inChennai-based AIWO, mentored by Aircel founder C Sivasankaran, runs physician-monitored longevity “Healthcation” programmes at The Leela Palace Chennai and Fairmont Mumbai. “No two people are alike. So why should their health programmes be the same? At AIWO, we bring together medical science, psychology, nutrition, sleep and recovery to create a personalised experience focused on measurable health outcomes,” says Sivasankaran.The promise is not only comfort but evidence. “We assess relevant health parameters before and after the programme so guests can understand their progress. All they need to do is arrive. Every aspect of their care and stay is thoughtfully curated and orchestrated around their individual needs,” he adds.Longevity-specific diagnostics can include biological age and epigenetic tests, genetic tests, physical fitness tests and advanced imaging, on top of the blood work a consultant prescribes before the retreat. At The Wellness Co’s clinics, samples are collected on site and sent to partner labs, and subscriptions start at a monthly tier ranging from ₹75,000 to ₹1 lakh for clinic membership. AIWO offers a programme called AIWO 360, a day of advanced diagnostics and preventive health planning for ₹1.3 lakh per person.Independent practitioners operating wellness and longevity clinics build their own toolkits, too. Tanya Malik Chawla, functional nutritionist, longevity researcher and founder of Biology By Design, often starts with simple blood markers that can be used to calculate phenotypic age. She also looks at functional strength and mobility markers such as VO2 Max, as well as hormonal markers. For digestive complaints, she may order gut microbiome tests or stool cultures, and for specialised cases, a genome panel, often tying up with testing labs and chains.Hospitality partners are important to the retreats to offer a premium luxury experience and manage the nutrition aspects; for the hotel owners, the appeal is a different kind of guest, one who stays from a week to 21 days. The Indian Hotels Company (IHCL), parent of Taj Hotels, entered the space in 2025 by acquiring a controlling stake in Atmantan Wellness Retreat, a luxury wellness centre at Mulshi in Pune, where programmes draw on ayurveda, yoga, Indian naturopathy, physiotherapy, nutrition, counselling, coaching and fitness. “At IHCL, we have always believed that the future of hospitality lies in anticipating evolving consumer aspirations and creating experiences that deliver enduring value. Wellness represents a significant opportunity in this landscape, with a growing focus on preventive health, longevity and overall well-being,” says Puneet Chhatwal, managing director and CEO of IHCL.Also Read: Our focus must shift to preventive, primary care: Kris GopalakrishnanHe adds that it takes more than a famous name. “From a business perspective, integrated wellness requires specialist expertise, a differentiated operating model and a long-term commitment to quality. IHCL brings to the partnership its strengths in hospitality, brand building and distribution, enabling Atmantan to build on its established foundation and reach a wider audience.”Akanksha Lamba, co-founder of The Postcard Hotel, says running a specialised retreat takes an entirely different set of competencies than running a luxury hotel. Standardising medical treatment and consultation protocols, she says, is key. Her hotel’s Ayurveda Retreat has partnered with Sitaram Ayurveda of Keralam to run a wellness and longevity retreat in Goa.“What is interesting about this segment is the decision to travel is driven by a very specific purpose,” says Lamba. That purpose shapes the property itself, because stays of a week to 21 days call for expansive natural surroundings and specialised design and architecture. It also makes for an intense operating model, requiring considerable manpower and attention to detail. “I believe the model is scalable, but it would be a mistake to approach it in the same way as expanding a conventional hotel portfolio,” she adds.The wellness companies on the other side of such partnerships carry a different burden. Most of their capital expenditure goes into machines and facilities for specialised treatments, and returns take a long time. Rishabh says revenue payback takes 18 to 24 months, depending on the city. “To be profitable it takes between 36 to 48 months though the numbers are coming down due to increasing awareness among people,” he adds.Patience, then, is required on both sides. The question is who the consumer for wellness and longevity treatment is. The pandemic, says Rishabh, was an inflection point for many Indians willing to invest in staying healthy for as long as possible, and the typical cohort at The Wellness Co clinics is between 35 and 58 years old. Malik Chawla dates the shift to the past decade, as more people want to take ownership of their health, and she sees the age range stretching further. “In addition to the cohort of people who are 35 years and above, I am seeing a lot of people over 60 years of age coming in who don’t want to rely on medication or supplements for their health issues,” she says. At retreats, traditional practices such as ayurveda, yoga and naturopathy find space alongside modern diagnostics, personalised nutrition and recovery therapiesWhat brings them in is rarely the same. “Every individual has their own definition of wellness. For some, it might be better hair and skin; for some, it would be getting rid of exhaustion; for others, it might be being able to fall asleep, and so on. It stems from what they are lacking or suffering from,” says Gaur.Also Read: Anti-ageing is a huge area. Everyone is jumping into it: Kiran Mazumdar-ShawThe young are still missing from that list. Dr Parvinder Kaur Chawla, senior consultant of internal medicine at Fortis Hospitals, Mohali, says the right age to build lifelong habits is childhood, yet most people recognise the need only in their 40s. “When you are in your 20s and 30s, your hormones are the engine, and you have a big buffer. Only when hormones start decreasing, do other symptoms show up. Most of the time, the younger ones come in only when pushed by their employers under the corporate programmes. We see that few people in their 30s and 40s actually come in with the intent of listening and changing their lifestyle,” she says. This kind of luxury, she adds, also requires financial and personal stability and access, which come later in the life cycle.Even for those who can afford it, the industry’s language needs careful reading. Malik Chawla cautions against taking biological age reversal to mean anti-ageing, and urges people to educate themselves on the difference. “Biology is plastic and is constantly changing. When we talk about age reversal, we are talking from a biological standpoint, and people end up misunderstanding it for anti-ageing. Reducing your biological age implies that your organs can function optimally, not the fact that you will never get wrinkles or grey hair.”Founders and doctors alike offer the same caution: There are no quick fixes. “The retreats open a window to better health. Many people don’t know about possibilities outside their own small world. However, a key determinant of whether you can reap lasting benefits from any retreat is whether you can continue with at least some of the lifestyle changes that you learnt at the retreat once you are back home,” says Kaur Chawla.So a retreat can surely be a gamechanger, provided guests bring a part of that retreat mentality home. For the industry, the bigger challenge as interest picks up may be the temptation to offer everything to everyone in one happy place.

stories.headline: Ghalibaf warns of "no negotiation" with US until Iran's seven conditions met
stories.title: Ghalibaf warns of "no negotiation" with US until Iran's seven conditions met
stories.summary: Tehran , November 24 : Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Tuesday warned that Iran will not take any action or enter into negotiations with the United States in order to end the hostilities in West Asia until its seven conditions are met, reiterating Tehran's position amid mounting tensions following fresh US sanctions targeting Iranian financial networks. In his remarks at the Iranian Parliament, Ghalibaf reiterated that Tehran's position remained unchanged and warned that the country was prepared to respond decisively to any hostile moves by its adversaries. "Our position is the same as we have said before: no action or negotiation will be taken before Iran implements its seven conditions, and we are ready to respond decisively to the enemy's movements and change the geography of the battle in the event of the enemy's mistake," Ghalibaf said. Addressing the recent threats from US President Donald Trump and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the Iranian Parliament Speaker, who is also the chief negotiator for the Islamic Republic, said that Washington's threats, insults and continued economic pressure against Iran reflected American helplessness. "In conclusion, and in the face of the recent nonsense and threats from the US President and Treasury Secretary, I need to clarify that our position is clear and unchangeable," he said. "The threats and insults to the proud and honourable people of Iran and the emphasis on economic pressure are, more than anything, a sign of the Americans' helplessness in the face of our beloved, resilient, and independent nation," Ghalibaf added. Ghalibaf's remarks came a day after the US Department of the Treasury announced that it had imposed sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies and key personnel as part of what it described as a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks. In a release on Monday, titled "Operation Economic Outcast Disrupts Iran's Global Shadow Banking Networks", the US Treasury said the action targeted financial infrastructure supporting much of Iran's remaining foreign trade. The department stated that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting exchange houses, front companies and facilitators that move billions of dollars through the international financial system to provide Iran with access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, commenting on the action in a post on X, said, "Iran’s economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking. Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime. Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake." According to the conditions outlined by Iran, Tehran is seeking the lifting of the US naval blockade on Iranian ports, sanctions relief, the release of frozen Iranian funds, an end to hostilities on all fronts and a formal declaration that the war is over. (ANI)

Addressing the recent threats from US President Donald Trump and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the Iranian Parliament Speaker, who is also the chief negotiator for the Islamic Republic, said that Washington's threats, insults and continued economic pressure against Iran reflected American helplessness.
"In conclusion, and in the face of the recent nonsense and threats from the US President and Treasury Secretary, I need to clarify that our position is clear and unchangeable," he said.

"The threats and insults to the proud and honourable people of Iran and the emphasis on economic pressure are, more than anything, a sign of the Americans' helplessness in the face of our beloved, resilient, and independent nation," Ghalibaf added.

Ghalibaf's remarks came a day after the US Department of the Treasury announced that it had imposed sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies and key personnel as part of what it described as a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks.

In a release on Monday, titled "Operation Economic Outcast Disrupts Iran's Global Shadow Banking Networks", the US Treasury said the action targeted financial infrastructure supporting much of Iran's remaining foreign trade.

The department stated that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting exchange houses, front companies and facilitators that move billions of dollars through the international financial system to provide Iran with access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, commenting on the action in a post on X, said, "Iran’s economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking.
Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime.

Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake." According to the conditions outlined by Iran, Tehran is seeking the lifting of the US naval blockade on Iranian ports, sanctions relief, the release of frozen Iranian funds, an end to hostilities on all fronts and a formal declaration that the war is over.

Addressing the recent threats from US President Donald Trump and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the Iranian Parliament Speaker, who is also the chief negotiator for the Islamic Republic, said that Washington's threats, insults and continued economic pressure against Iran reflected American helplessness.

stories.headline: More than 2.36 million end-of-life vehicles plying in Delhi-NCR: CAQM to Supreme Court
stories.title: More than 2.36 million end-of-life vehicles plying in Delhi-NCR: CAQM to Supreme Court
stories.summary: The Commission submitted that older vehicles emit considerably higher quantities of pollutants than those conforming to Bharat Stage-VI norms
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) has told the Supreme Court that more than 2.36 million end-of-life vehicles are plying on roads across Delhi-NCR.

An end-of-life vehicle is a vehicle that can no longer be legally registered or operated on public roads due to age limits, failed fitness tests, cancelled registration, severe damage, or voluntary surrender by its owner.

In its affidavit filed in the Supreme Court, the CAQM said that of the 2.54 million overage vehicles reported across Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, only 1.85 lakh had been scrapped or issued no-objection certificates.
The affidavit was submitted in a suo motu case examining the regulatory framework governing air pollution.
The Commission said two-wheelers account for 65.2% of the total vehicle population in Delhi-NCR, while four-wheeler light motor vehicles comprise another 28.9%.
The Commission submitted that older vehicles emit considerably higher quantities of pollutants than those conforming to Bharat Stage-VI norms.

Detailing the steps taken to control pollution, the CAQM said it has directed that only CNG, electric or BS-VI diesel inter-city buses be allowed to enter Delhi from November 1, 2026, including buses operating under All India Tourist Permits.

Similarly, commercial goods vehicles other than BS-VI, CNG, LNG and electric vehicles have been barred from entering Delhi from November 1, 2026, subject to the applicable exemptions, the commission informed the Supreme Court.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Issues Notice On PIL Against MPs/MLAs Resigning To Evade Anti-Defection Law
stories.title: Supreme Court Issues Notice On PIL Against MPs/MLAs Resigning To Evade Anti-Defection Law
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Monday (November 23) issued notice on a PIL seeking safeguards against Members of Parliament and State Legislatures using strategically timed resignations to avoid disqualification proceedings under the 10th Schedule of the Constitution (the anti-defection law).
A Bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana sought responses of the Union Government, the Election Commission of India, the Law Commission of India.
Senior Advocate A. Sirajudeen appeared for the petitioner (A Sethu).

The case has been tagged with another plea raising the issue of election expenditure recovery from a candidate who resigns after getting elected from one political party in order to recontest from another party (Ref: K Suthan.
Union of India).

The PIL raises concerns that legislators facing/anticipating disqualification proceedings frequently tender their resignations before the Speaker or Chairman of the House can adjudicate the allegations of defection on merits.

It contends that such resignations, alongwith prolonged delays in disposal of disqualification petitions, enable legislators to evade the consequences contemplated under the 10th Schedule and facilitate political realignments that may alter the fate of elected governments.
Referring to Shrimanth Balasaheb Patil.

Hon'ble Speaker, Karnataka Legislative Assembly, the petitioner argues that resignation and disqualification operate in distinct constitutional fields and that resignation after a disqualifying act does not extinguish proceedings relating to alleged defection.

"A resignation process that can be used to postpone, and then to avoid, the consequences of defection, coupled with the absence of any enforced time-limit for deciding disqualification petitions, impairs the integrity of the electoral mandate”, the plea states.

It is further the petitioner's contention that by the time disqualification proceedings are eventually decided, the term of the House may have expired, a by-election may have taken place, or the Government may have fallen or survived, thereby rendering the adjudication ineffective.
The petitioner relies upon the Supreme Court's decisions in Kihoto Hollohan.
